newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: FEATURE - Turkmenistan leader's cult alive and well.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Turkmenistan leader's cult alive and well.

text.p: More than five years after Turkmenistan won independence from Moscow, President Saparmurat Niyazov is enjoying the kind of personality cult that would have made even former Soviet dictator Josef Stalin proud.

Opposition parties are banned, portraits of the president keep watch from every street corner and the population of around four million is simply too afraid to express publicly what it really thinks about the leader and his extravagant ways.
As Niyazov surrounds himself in splendour befitting a king, his people, proud descendants of Turkic nomads, struggle to get by on wages that average just $18 a month.
The government has promised that better times lie ahead, saying huge oil and gas reserves lying under the country's desert terrain will turn it into another Kuwait one day.
Such pledges fail to convince many ordinary Turkmen.
"There is oil, there is gas, and there are only four million people living here," said a taxi driver who asked not to be identified.
"But the president and his entourage just put everything in their pockets and leave."

Situated between the impoverished former Soviet republics Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan to the north and internationally unpopular Iran and Afghanistan to the south, getting oil and gas to hard cash markets is likely to take years.
But Niyazov is likely to be still in charge when the money finally starts to flow.
His presidency was extended to 2002 by a referendum in 1994, a decision officials have said had the blessing of more than 90 percent of the population.
WHEREVER YOU GO, TURKMENBASHI IS WATCHING
In a throw-back to Soviet times, Niyazov, more widely known as Turkmenbashi or "head of the Turkmens", keeps a close eye on his people.
"He's watching you wherever you go," said a second taxi driver, who asked to be identified only as Murat.
Visitors stepping off the plane are greeted by a gold-plated portrait of the 57-year-old president alongside the Soviet-style inscription "We must glorify our motherland."
A huge poster of him hangs near the approach to the airport from the capital Ashgabat to bid them farewell when they leave.

Photographs of the stocky, silver-haired Niyazov adorn every official building and many more besides. In the four-star Aziya hotel on the outskirts of the capital, a huge portrait hangs at the head of the main staircase.
Even out of sight Turkmenbashi's presence is felt, not least through his highly visible police force.
"There are police everywhere - it's like the KGB used to be in Russia," Murat said.
TURKMENS WONDER AT PRESIDENT'S EXTRAVAGANCE
With such a strong grip on power, Niyazov can afford to fill his plate as his people fight over scraps from the table.
A huge palace, surrounded by formal gardens and flood-lit fountains, is being built in the centre of the capital. One local reporter said it would cost between $80 million and $85 million.

Much larger sums were spent on erecting around 30 four and five-star hotels on a long stretch of road on the outskirts of Ashgabat. Not even a major international oil and gas conference held earlier this month could get close to filling them.
At one end of the "millionaire mile", as one local called it, a huge museum is under construction.
"The National Museum is a present to the inhabitants of Turkmenistan from Saparmurat Turkmenbashi," a large sign outside declares proudly.
"We'd be better off getting higher pay," the local said.
"It's getting better in that there are a lot of new buildings sprouting up which makes the place look better. But for the average Turkmen, life is still difficult," Murat added.
PEOPLE IMPROVISE TO SUBSIDISE PALTRY WAGE
Many Turkmens have either lost or left their jobs and turned to private means to earn money. Those with cars often cruise the dusty streets of Ashgabat acting as unofficial taxis.
"I am an engineer with a good education, and in Soviet times I had a job," said one driver.
"But then all the firms shut down. It's a good thing I have a car, as otherwise I couldn't feed my kids."
Niyazov promised to double salaries to state-paid employees and the military in February, funding the increase from payment of gas arrears by other former Soviet republics.
But some citizens said real benefits would be minimal.
"Tukmenbashi promised wages would go up, forgetting to add that prices in shops go up twice as fast," said a market trader.
Bazaars in the capital have sprouted up, offering a wider choice of food and clothes than half-empty state shops. But again they are out of reach for many.
"In state shops there is nothing, and in bazaars you have to pay world prices, so how can we afford it?" one shopper said.
STEELED FOR FURTHER HARDSHIPS
"What can we do but grin and bear it?" asked one taxi driver. "The nearest opponents to Turkmenbashi are in Moscow, and we can't even get Russian newspapers to keep in touch with the outside world.
"It's as if we were completely blind."
Despite Niyazov's promises, miracle cures are not expected any time soon.
"The only people life gets better for are the people in power or those close to them," Murat said.
"It will be many years before it gets any better for us."
